questions.prompt: What is the main job of the @State property wrapper in SwiftUI?

options.text: It creates a local source of truth owned by one view.
options.explanation: Right. @State sets up a view-local source of truth.

options.text: It shares global database records across all app screens.
options.explanation: @State holds local UI state for one view, not global databases.

options.text: It turns Swift functions into background worker queues.
options.explanation: @State stores view data; it does not create background queues.

options.text: It stops SwiftUI from recreating the view struct on redraw.
options.explanation: SwiftUI still recreates the struct, while keeping @State in separate memory.

questions.prompt: Why does Apple recommend marking @State properties as private?

options.text: To stop the property from compiling on older iOS versions.
options.explanation: Marking a property private does not change iOS version support.

options.text: To make sure only the owning view can change its source of truth.
options.explanation: Right. private keeps outside views from changing local state directly.

options.text: To lock the variable inside the iPhone hardware security chip.
options.explanation: @State stores UI state in memory; it does not use hardware chips.

options.text: To force SwiftUI to save the value directly to disk files.
options.explanation: @State lives in memory while the view exists and is not saved to disk.

questions.prompt: What does a @Binding property wrapper stand for in SwiftUI?

options.text: A saved copy of data kept inside the device settings file.
options.explanation: @Binding does not store its own data or save settings to disk.

options.text: A background worker that watches for network responses.
options.explanation: @Binding connects view data; it does not run network tasks.

options.text: A two-way connection to data owned by another view.
options.explanation: Right. @Binding reads and writes data owned by another source of truth.

options.text: A custom animation curve for moving between app screens.
options.explanation: @Binding shares state between views, not animation curves.

questions.prompt: What does the dollar sign ($) prefix return when used on an @State property?

options.text: It prints the memory address of the property as a hex number.
options.explanation: $ reads the projected value, not a raw memory address.

options.text: It formats the stored number as a local money string.
options.explanation: Money formatting uses formatters, not the $ property wrapper prefix.

options.text: It deletes the property from memory to run garbage collection.
options.explanation: Swift manages memory automatically without garbage collection.

options.text: It reads the projected value, returning a Binding to the data.
options.explanation: Right. On an @State variable, the $ prefix returns a Binding.

questions.prompt: Where does SwiftUI keep the actual value of an @State property?

options.text: In persistent memory managed outside the short-lived view struct.
options.explanation: Right. SwiftUI keeps @State values in separate memory tied to the view.

options.text: Inside the view struct itself just like normal let properties.
options.explanation: If stored inside the struct, state would reset on every redraw.

options.text: Inside the app UserDefaults file saved on the device storage.
options.explanation: UserDefaults saves data to disk, while @State lives in memory.

options.text: Inside GPU image buffers built for fast screen drawing.
options.explanation: UI state values live in system memory, not GPU image buffers.

questions.prompt: What happens when an @State value changes while the app is running?

options.text: SwiftUI stops the app right away with a state error.
options.explanation: Changing @State is normal and updates the UI.

options.text: SwiftUI marks the view dirty and runs var body again to update it.
options.explanation: Right. State changes trigger SwiftUI to update any view reading that state.

options.text: The whole app window is rebuilt from scratch at startup.
options.explanation: Only the views that depend on the changed state are updated.

options.text: SwiftUI freezes the main thread until background tasks finish.
options.explanation: SwiftUI does not pause the main thread when state changes.

sources.title: Apple Developer Documentation: Managing user interface state

questions.prompt: Why is initializing @State inside a view's custom init from a parameter a mistake?

options.text: Because Swift structs are not allowed to have init parameters.
options.explanation: Structs can have custom initializers with parameters normally.

options.text: Because initializers always run on background worker threads.
options.explanation: View initializers run on the caller thread, not automatically in the background.

options.text: Because SwiftUI keeps the old state and ignores new init values.
options.explanation: Right. SwiftUI creates @State memory once, so later init values are ignored.

options.text: Because calling init on a View struct creates a retain cycle.
options.explanation: Structs are value types and do not form reference retain cycles.

questions.prompt: What happens if you change an @State variable directly inside var body?

options.text: The view draws twice as fast because SwiftUI skips diffing.
options.explanation: Changing state inside body causes redraw loops, not faster drawing.

options.text: The new value is ignored and resets back to its starting value.
options.explanation: The change happens and triggers another body call right away.

options.text: The compiler moves the state change onto a background queue.
options.explanation: The compiler does not move body code to background queues.

options.text: It triggers runtime warnings and repeated redraw loops.
options.explanation: Right. Changing @State during body causes repeated redraws and warnings.

questions.prompt: How can you supply a sample binding value inside a #Preview block?

options.text: By using Binding.constant(value) to pass a fixed binding.
options.explanation: Right. Binding.constant creates a fixed binding that works well in previews.

options.text: By passing nil to skip the binding parameter during previews.
options.explanation: Binding is not optional, so you cannot pass nil directly.

options.text: By creating a global class that inherits from UIView.
options.explanation: Binding.constant is the standard simple way to preview bindings.

options.text: By calling a previewBinding() macro above the child view.
options.explanation: SwiftUI has no previewBinding macro; use Binding.constant.

questions.prompt: What happens when a child view changes a @Binding property?

options.text: The child updates a local copy and sends a UIKit notification.
options.explanation: Bindings do not send UIKit notifications; they write to the source of truth.

options.text: The binding writes straight to the parent source of truth.
options.explanation: Right. Changing a binding updates the original @State value in the parent.

options.text: The change waits until the user puts the app in the background.
options.explanation: Binding changes update the parent state right away on the main thread.

options.text: The parent view receives a brand new copy of the whole view tree.
options.explanation: Bindings update the shared source of truth without copying view trees.

questions.prompt: What kind of data belongs in a view's @State property?

options.text: Large shared databases holding every customer order in the app.
options.explanation: Shared app models belong in @Observable models or storage layers.

options.text: Global network clients shared by twenty different app screens.
options.explanation: Shared services belong in @Observable models or the environment.

options.text: Local UI values like button toggles, text input, and counters.
options.explanation: Right. @State is made for view-local UI state.

options.text: Long-running background GPS logs shared across app extensions.
options.explanation: Shared background services do not belong in one view's @State.

questions.prompt: How does SwiftUI achieve unidirectional data flow with @State and @Binding?

options.text: By forcing all child views to talk through NotificationCenter.
options.explanation: SwiftUI passes values and bindings down instead of global notifications.

options.text: By blocking child views from ever changing any parent data.
options.explanation: Child views can update parent state through two-way bindings.

options.text: By saving all screen values inside one global singleton dictionary.
options.explanation: SwiftUI keeps local sources of truth with @State, not global dictionaries.

options.text: State flows down as values or bindings, and actions flow back up.
options.explanation: Right. State passes down the view tree and user actions update it upward.

questions.prompt: How can you create a custom Binding with your own get and set logic?

options.text: By calling Binding(get:set:) with getter and setter closures.
options.explanation: Right. Binding(get:set:) creates a custom binding from closures.

options.text: By subclassing @State inside a new custom UIView class.
options.explanation: State and Binding are structs, so you cannot subclass them.

options.text: By overloading the $ symbol with a custom math operator.
options.explanation: The $ prefix reads a property wrapper's projected value; it is not an operator.

options.text: By writing a Swift extension that overrides wrappedValue as let.
options.explanation: You build custom bindings with Binding(get:set:), not by overriding wrappedValue.

questions.prompt: What happens if you pass an @State variable without the $ prefix to a child?

options.text: The child gets a two-way binding that edits the parent state.
options.explanation: Passing without $ sends a read-only value, not a binding.

options.text: The child gets a read-only copy of the current state value.
options.explanation: Right. count passes the Int value; $count passes a Binding.

options.text: The Swift compiler fails with a syntax error every time.
options.explanation: Passing a state value as a read-only parameter is valid and common.

options.text: The parent state resets back to its starting value right away.
options.explanation: Passing a read-only value does not reset parent state.

questions.prompt: How does @Binding differ from a standard Swift inout parameter?

options.text: inout lives across screen redraws, while @Binding runs once.
options.explanation: It is the opposite: inout lasts for one call, while @Binding works across redraws.

options.text: inout requires a class reference, while @Binding only wraps Int.
options.explanation: Both inout and @Binding work with value types like Int, Bool, and String.

options.text: @Binding works across view redraws, while inout lasts for one call.
options.explanation: Right. Binding is a struct wrapper that stays valid across UI redraws; inout lasts one call.

options.text: There is no difference; both keywords do the exact same thing.
options.explanation: @Binding is a SwiftUI property wrapper, while inout is a function parameter keyword.

questions.prompt: Explain the difference between @State and @Binding in SwiftUI. Write 2 to 5 sentences.

rubric.criterion: Explains that @State owns a local source of truth stored outside the view struct.
Explains that @Binding is a two-way connection to data owned elsewhere without storing its own copy.

questions.modelAnswer: @State creates a local source of truth owned by one view. SwiftUI keeps @State data in persistent memory outside the short-lived view struct. In contrast, @Binding stores no data of its own. It gives a child view a two-way connection to read and change data owned by another view.

questions.prompt: Why should @State properties always be marked private? Write 2 to 5 sentences.

rubric.criterion: Explains that @State holds data owned locally by that view.
States that marking it private keeps outside views from changing it directly.

questions.modelAnswer: @State is meant to hold internal state owned by one view. Marking @State as private protects that data from outside views. It stops another view from passing a bad value or changing the state directly. If a child view needs to edit that data, pass a @Binding with $ instead.

questions.prompt: What does the dollar sign ($) prefix mean on an @State property, and how is it used? Write 2 to 5 sentences.

rubric.criterion: Identifies $ as syntax that reads the projected value of a property wrapper.
Explains that on @State, the projected value returns a Binding.
Gives an example of passing the binding to a child view or control like Toggle or TextField.

questions.modelAnswer: The $ prefix reads the projected value of a property wrapper. For an @State property, that projected value returns a Binding pointing to the stored data. You pass it to child views or controls like Toggle or TextField so they can read and change the parent state. For example, passing $isOn lets a Toggle flip the parent's Bool.

questions.prompt: Why is initializing @State inside a view's custom init from a parameter a mistake, and what should you do instead? Write 2 to 5 sentences.

rubric.criterion: Explains that SwiftUI sets up @State memory only once when the view first enters the screen.
States that later parent redraws passing new values to init are ignored.
Recommends passing a plain let property or a @Binding instead.

questions.modelAnswer: SwiftUI creates @State storage only once when the view first enters the screen. If you set @State from an init parameter, later parent redraws with new values are ignored. SwiftUI keeps reusing the first stored value instead of updating it. If a child view must follow changing parent values, pass a plain let property or a @Binding.

questions.prompt: Explain how @State and @Binding support unidirectional data flow in SwiftUI. Write 2 to 5 sentences.

rubric.criterion: Explains that state flows down from a source of truth as values or bindings.
Explains that user actions flow upward through bindings to update the source of truth.
States that changing @State triggers SwiftUI to redraw affected views.

questions.modelAnswer: SwiftUI follows unidirectional data flow by keeping one clear source of truth. The parent owns the state with @State and passes read-only values or @Binding connections down to child views. When a user acts in a child view, the change flows upward through the binding to update the parent's state. SwiftUI then redraws any views that depend on that state.
